newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala military police rise up over peace pact.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala military police rise up over peace pact.

text.p: About 1,000 armed Guatemalan military police on Thursday defied their commanders and seized their own compound in the first army rebellion against terms of a peace treaty signed last month.
Protesting soldiers toting machineguns manned lookout posts on the compound's perimeter wall, and roadblocks made of tires were put up in surrounding streets.
While there was no fighting or violence some politicians feared the revolt posed a threat to the fragile peace accord.
"This is pretty worrying because it is an attempt against the peace treaty," Congressman Gumercindo Donis, president of the Congressional National Defence Committee, told reporters.
The protesters were demanding severance pay when the 4,000-strong military police (PMA) is dissolved this year as part of government promises to leftist rebels.

Protesters complained that the guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit had won a better deal in the peace accords. That concern was shared by officers, who while not part of the rebellion, were in the compound in apparent sympathy with their men.
"The government is obtaining help for the guerrillas and not for us," said Lt.-Col. Escriba, who refused to give his first name, as he milled around in the 1,500-man barracks.
"They were demeaning us, marginalizing us without any rights. While they don't give us money, we won't hand over our arms," one soldier told Reuters.
It was the first such protest by the country's powerful army since the Dec. 29 peace treaty that ended a 36-year war in which 140,000 Guatemalans died or disappeared.

Protesters said they would maintain their stand "to the bitter end." They said they had given the government 48 hours to reach a negotiated solution, but did not spell out what would happen if their demands were ignored.
The government pledged in the peace treaty to cut the armed forces by a third. The army has played a pivotal, and at times brutal, role in political life For much of Guatemala's recent history.

Army spokesman Otto Noack said the peace agreements clearly stated that all demobilized army personnel would receive government aid for a "productive return" to civilian life, but they did not set a specific severance pay.
"That is the big worry of the people who work in the PMA, how much their severance pay or benefits will be," he said.
The protest began late on Wednesday when the military policemen refused to turn in their arms after work and took over the fortified compound in northern Guatemala City.
Most of the urban military policemen work around the city during the day, providing security at banks, government buildings and private businesses.
During the protest some of the police stopped traffic on streets around the compound and harangued drivers. They demanded negotiations with the government, asking for $6,600 to $8,300 severance pay.
"I am sure that you will not have to leave empty-handed," said Gen. Manuel Ventura of the Defence Ministry, who arrived on Thursday at the compound to negotiate with the protesters.
